item.title: [70★] Entropic measures of quantum information
item.author: Roberto Rubboli, ..., Ludovico Lami, Marco Tomamichel
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 70 ★

Authors: Roberto Rubboli, ..., Ludovico Lami, Marco Tomamichel

arXiv ID: 2611.08254 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Entropy has played a pivotal role in physics ever since its inception by Clausius in the early industrial age. Shannon ushered the concept into the information age by using it to describe fundamental limits of information processing, founding the field of information theory. Today, a fruitful interaction between information theory and physics is pushing our understanding of entropy forward. It has revealed, in particular, that no single notion of entropy suffices to capture all relevant properties of physical systems, making it necessary to consider a variety of entropic measures of quantum information, each with distinct features and uses. This review surveys these recent advances in a structured way, covering a comprehensive array of information measures, including Rényi and smooth entropies, together with their interrelations. Starting with a systematic characterization of entropies that motivates their definitions from natural physical principles, we discuss their applications ranging from quantum communication and cryptography to resource theories, thermodynamics, and many-body physics.

Roberto Rubboli, ..., Ludovico Lami, Marco Tomamichel

item.title: [54★] Polynomial-time classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss
item.author: Armando Angrisani, Hela Mhiri
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 54 ★

Authors: Armando Angrisani, Hela Mhiri

arXiv ID: 2611.08444 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Sampling experiments are a leading approach to demonstrating quantum computational advantage, yet their robustness to experimental noise is not completely understood. We develop a common framework for classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss, including pure loss. For Fock-state boson sampling, Gaussian boson sampling with fixed uniform squeezing, and fermion sampling with magic inputs, we obtain polynomial-time sampling at inverse-polynomial total variation error, for any fixed nonzero overall loss rate, and with high probability over Haar-random interferometers. A milder flatness assumption on the ideal output distribution suffices for quasipolynomial-time simulation without Haar randomness. With constant thermal loss per layer, the same flatness assumption gives polynomial-time simulation at logarithmic depth. Our bounds for Fock-state boson sampling cover both dilute and saturated regimes and become stronger near full input filling: when only a bounded number of input modes are empty, the noisy output for Haar-random interferometers converges, as the number of modes grows, to a distribution independent of the interferometer.

Armando Angrisani, Hela Mhiri

item.title: [39★] Frustration-freeness is decidable but unprovable
item.author: Naoto Shiraishi
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 39 ★

Authors: Naoto Shiraishi

arXiv ID: 2611.07337 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The frustration-free property is valuable in quantum many-body systems, which states that its ground states simultaneously minimize all local interaction terms, even when these terms act on overlapping degrees of freedom. Prominent examples include the AKLT model and Kitaev's toric code model, which serve as paradigmatic models of symmetry-protected topological phases and topological order, respectively. A fundamental question is whether a given Hamiltonian is frustration-free for all system sizes. Here we establish two seemingly contradictory results concerning this decision problem. First, we prove that frustration-freeness is decidable for any fixed local Hilbert space dimension. Specifically, there exists a finite, Hamiltonian-independent system-size cutoff such that frustration-freeness at this cutoff size guarantees frustration-freeness at all system sizes. Second, on the other hand, we also show that there exists a frustration-free Hamiltonian whose frustration-freeness cannot be proved within the standard axioms of mathematics (ZFC). We reconcile these seemingly contradictory results by showing that the cutoff, although finite for each local Hilbert space dimension, is uncomputable as a function of that dimension. Our findings reveal an unexpected fundamental distinction between decidability and provability arising in quantum many-body physics.

Naoto Shiraishi

item.title: [30★] Certifying quantum code and circuit distances at scale
item.author: Bin Cheng, Naixu Guo, Feng Pan
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 30 ★

Authors: Bin Cheng, Naixu Guo, Feng Pan

arXiv ID: 2611.08247 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Code and circuit distances characterize how strongly quantum error correction suppresses logical errors and guide code comparisons, schedule choices and resource estimates. Yet many published distances are only upper bounds from heuristic searches. Here, we express both distances as tropical partition functions and evaluate them with rank-based dynamic programming and weight-bounded search. Circuit reductions and relaxations shrink the problems, and proved lower bounds with explicit logical errors of matching weight certify exact values. On two benchmarks, our method certifies more instances than all other tested exact solvers combined. We certify distances for codes with up to 31,200 qubits, such as Google's modular hyperbolic codes, and for memory circuits with up to 8×1058×1058\times10^5 fault mechanisms, such as those of high-rate Cornucopia codes. Our audit of 26 recent papers identifies overestimated distances and non-tight upper bounds in 10 papers, with a maximum discrepancy of at least eight. Certified distances also guide circuit design and show which defective chips remain usable. In particular, we certify circuit distance 16 for IBM's two-gross memory circuits with the standard schedule, not the assumed 18, whereas redesigned schedules reach 18 at one noisy cycle, at the cost of one more timestep per cycle. At 99.98% junction yield, keeping gross-code memory blocks with dead checks that are certified at distance 10 or more raises the estimated usable share from 53% for perfect blocks alone to 94% with an improved schedule.

Bin Cheng, Naixu Guo, Feng Pan

item.title: [25★] Provable circuit-level thresholds for non-abelian topological phases
item.author: Yuanjie Ren, ..., Shankar Balasubramanian, Andreas Bauer
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 25 ★

Authors: Yuanjie Ren, ..., Shankar Balasubramanian, Andreas Bauer

arXiv ID: 2611.08488 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We provide an explicit scheme to realize a quantum memory in any 2D non-chiral topological order. For this, we construct syndrome extraction circuits based on the Turaev-Viro path integral as well as a classical algorithm for decoding on the fly. We prove that our scheme has a threshold under a local stochastic circuit-level noise model and discuss how to generalize it to implement topological logical gates.

Yuanjie Ren, ..., Shankar Balasubramanian, Andreas Bauer

item.title: [21★] Machine learning quantum data to accelerate quantum Monte Carlo
item.author: Tong Jiang, ..., William J. Huggins, Joonho Lee
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 21 ★

Authors: Tong Jiang, ..., William J. Huggins, Joonho Lee

arXiv ID: 2611.08151 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Simulating strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials remains a central goal for quantum computing. A promising strategy uses quantum processors to prepare trial wavefunctions that guide classical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, the enormous computational cost of repeatedly processing quantum measurements has severely limited the practical scalability of this approach. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by compressing quantum measurement data into machine-learning models that efficiently provide the wavefunction overlaps needed by QMC. This accelerates quantum-classical QMC by orders of magnitude, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations with comparable accuracy. We demonstrate our approach on hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters using measurements from Google's Willow processor. By enabling efficient reuse of quantum-state information on the classical coprocessor, our framework addresses a fundamental bottleneck in hybrid quantum algorithms that will persist even into the fault-tolerant era.

Tong Jiang, ..., William J. Huggins, Joonho Lee

item.title: [19★] Single-shot ground-state preparation via strongly coupled baths
item.author: Liang-Hong Mo, ..., Dmitry A. Abanin, Biao Lian
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 19 ★

Authors: Liang-Hong Mo, ..., Dmitry A. Abanin, Biao Lian

arXiv ID: 2611.07021 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Preparing ground and thermal states of quantum many-body systems is a central task in quantum simulation. Dissipative protocols have emerged as a promising solution for both near-term and fault-tolerant hardware, but most constructions rely on weak system-bath coupling, leading to slow cooling. Here, we construct cooling protocols at strong system-bath coupling, and demonstrate accurate state preparation within even a single cooling cycle. Our protocols combine dynamically ramped ancilla energy levels with time-dependent couplings to optimize the trade-off between cooling error and physical time. For a general class of free-fermion systems, we reduce the dynamics exactly to a two-level scattering problem: ground-state cooling becomes a control problem of maximizing resonant excitation transfer while suppressing non-adiabatic heating. We then construct a family of ``Möbius-Ingham'' protocols, which reach optimal error scaling for gapless spectra and almost-exponential suppression of the leading heating error for gapped spectra, as a function of the cycle period. In our free-fermion benchmarks, Möbius-Ingham cooling lies on the Pareto frontier between steady-state error and cooling time among the controls tested. We further demonstrate its effectiveness in interacting Ising and tt-VV chains and the two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model. Finally, we extend our construction to Gibbs state preparation, showing how free-fermion thermal states can be prepared in a single cycle.

Liang-Hong Mo, ..., Dmitry A. Abanin, Biao Lian

item.title: [16★] Dualities in one-dimensional quantum lattice models: Lie groups, Schur-Weyl duality and symmetry breaking
item.author: Dante Bosgoed, Frank Verstraete, Laurens Lootens
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 16 ★

Authors: Dante Bosgoed, Frank Verstraete, Laurens Lootens

arXiv ID: 2611.08293 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We present a systematic framework for gauging continuous symmetries, and show that the Schur-Weyl duality arises naturally as a realization of this construction with open boundary conditions. Restricting to compact Lie group symmetries, we construct dual models for one-dimensional quantum lattice models exhibiting those symmetries. We demonstrate that matrix product operators enable the explicit construction of intertwiners between the dual theories and their (non-invertible) symmetries. With closed boundary conditions, we can relate the full spectrum of these dual theories by considering all possible twisted boundary conditions.We illustrate how the Peter-Weyl transform appears when the duality acts on the boundary Hilbert space of a GG-symmetric model. The presented framework generalizes previous work on dualities for unitary fusion category symmetric models. It exemplifies how dualities for both finite and continuous symmetries rely on the relation between a bond algebra and a representation of the symmetry in the lattice as double centralizers. We argue that dual non-invertible spontaneous symmetry breaking is the mechanism that underlies symmetric tensor network algorithms. We illustrate these results for U(1)U(1)- and SU(2)SU(2)-symmetric quantum lattice models.

Dante Bosgoed, Frank Verstraete, Laurens Lootens

item.title: [16★] Quantum Advantage with Sign-Free Proofs: An Oracle Separation between StoqMA\mathsf{StoqMA} and MA\mathsf{MA}
item.author: Yassine Hamoudi, Yvan Le Borgne, Shrinidhi Teganahally Sridhara
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 16 ★

Authors: Yassine Hamoudi, Yvan Le Borgne, Shrinidhi Teganahally Sridhara

arXiv ID: 2611.08180 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Several landmark oracle results (FOCS 2000, FOCS 2025, STOC 2026) establish strict separations along the chain MA⊆QCMA⊆QMA\mathsf{MA} \subseteq \mathsf{QCMA} \subseteq \mathsf{QMA}, showing that quantum verification and quantum witnesses can each provide additional power over classical proof systems. These separations, however, use substantial coherent quantum computation, often through the quantum Fourier transform. We prove that a minimal quantum resource already suffices to outperform every classical verifier. Namely, we show the separation \mathsfMA⊊\mathsfStoqMA\mathsfMA ⊊\mathsfStoqMA relative to a classical oracle. The class StoqMA\mathsf{StoqMA}, introduced by Bravyi, Bessen, and Terhal (arXiv 2006), restricts the verifier to classical reversible computation, followed by a single Hadamard-basis measurement. Its power is closely tied to the complexity of stoquastic Hamiltonians, a sign-problem-free and seemingly more tractable class of quantum Hamiltonians. Our separating problem is to determine whether a sparse high-girth graph, given via an adjacency-list oracle, has a large or small Perron--Frobenius eigenvalue. This amounts to a ground-energy estimation task for a related stoquastic Hamiltonian. Our construction builds on a line of work on graph exploration problems with exponential quantum speedups, from welded trees (STOC 2003) to recent constructions (STOC 2021, arXiv 2026).

Yassine Hamoudi, Yvan Le Borgne, Shrinidhi Teganahally Sridhara

item.title: [15★] Extensions of the Haldane gap proof: higher dimensions, near degeneracy, fermions and tensor-network states
item.author: Tarun Grover
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 15 ★

Authors: Tarun Grover

arXiv ID: 2611.07400 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

A recent remarkable paper by OpenAI showed that the spin-one Heisenberg chain with periodic boundary conditions has a spectral gap in the thermodynamic limit. The proof elegantly deduces this gap from the Hamiltonian's spectrum on a finite system. This basic idea is an inequality involving the purity of the original Gibbs state and a dual Gibbs state that is defined via space-time rotation. Here we consider a few generalizations of this purity bootstrap argument. We first extend it to arbitrary spatial dimensions. Our main result uses the space-time duality between symmetry generators and symmetry twists to obtain upper bounds on the splitting of nearly degenerate low-energy states, together with a nonzero gap above them, from finite-system information. As applications, we show that finite-system calculations for the 2+1-D toric code in a field and the 2+1-D transverse-field Ising model establish parameter regimes with four and two low-lying states whose splittings are bounded from above by e−cLe^{-cL} and e−cL2e^{-cL^2} respectively for arbitrarily large system size LL, while the gap above these states remains nonzero in the thermodynamic limit. Next, we extend it to fermionic systems and use a finite calculation to establish a symmetric mass generation phase in a 2+12+1-D fermionic model. Finally, we apply the bootstrap to tensor-network states and establish exponential decay of connected correlations of all local operators in the symmetric square-lattice spin-one state introduced by Jian and Zaletel.

Tarun Grover

item.title: [14★] Physical regimes of quartic quantum advantage in elastic media simulation
item.author: David Jennings, ..., Matteo Lostaglio, Tamás Vaszary
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 14 ★

Authors: David Jennings, ..., Matteo Lostaglio, Tamás Vaszary

arXiv ID: 2611.06975 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum algorithms for elastic media simulation have been conjectured to offer up to a quartic quantum advantage over classical methods; however, the devil is always in the details. Here, we determine key physical conditions under which this quartic separation could be achieved in the relevant parameters. For continuum elastic dynamics at fixed volume with spatial convergence order mm, we find that the end-to-end speedup is of order (m+4)/(m+1)(m+4)/(m+1) in the simulation time, and 4/(m+1)4/(m+1) in the accuracy, with exponential memory advantage. For elastic lattice systems, we define microscopically resolved bulk observables (MRBOs) as those that can be efficiently extracted from a quantum state, but cannot be resolved by a known continuum model with fewer degrees of freedom than the lattice. We then argue that the estimation of MRBOs is a candidate problem for quartic quantum advantage in problem size. We propose MRBOs for pseudorandom heterogeneous materials as an explicit end-to-end application where this occurs, while admitting efficient `quantum cheese' encodings of the material properties. We thus demonstrate how the interplay between regularity, physical scale, observable sensitivity and quantum encodability constrains the relation between classical and quantum complexity.

David Jennings, ..., Matteo Lostaglio, Tamás Vaszary

item.title: [13★] Certifying the Rydberg-exposure limit of a globally driven controlled-Z gate
item.author: Yusheng Zhao, ..., Jie Wang, Jinguo Liu
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 13 ★

Authors: Yusheng Zhao, ..., Jie Wang, Jinguo Liu

arXiv ID: 2611.07388 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Rydberg excitation enables entangling gates in neutral-atom quantum processors but also exposes them to spontaneous decay. Whether this exposure can be made arbitrarily small through pulse shaping and longer gate times has remained unresolved. We show that an exact controlled-ZZ gate driven by a single global laser has an irreducible Rydberg-exposure cost in the perfect-blockade regime. The product of the maximum Rabi frequency Ωmax\Omega_{\max} and the average time TRT_R spent in the Rydberg state is bounded below by 2.93122.9312, independent of pulse shape and duration. We derive this bound using a sum-of-squares certificate, strengthened by constraints imposed by the shared drive. Using interval arithmetic, we also certify the existence of an exact gate pulse with ΩmaxTR<2.9359\Omega_{max} T_R<2.9359. The unrounded bounds differ by less than 0.16%0.16\%. The bound identifies a fundamental cost of shared-drive entangling dynamics and establishes a benchmark against which future gate-control strategies can be assessed.

Yusheng Zhao, ..., Jie Wang, Jinguo Liu

item.title: [10★] Monopoles, Scattering and Generalized Symmetries on a Quantum Computer
item.author: Oliver O'Brien, ..., Henrik Dreyer, Frank Verstraete
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 10 ★

Authors: Oliver O'Brien, ..., Henrik Dreyer, Frank Verstraete

arXiv ID: 2611.07960 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum computers have advanced to the stage that interesting many-body quantum phenomena can be observed. A striking example is the magnetic monopole paradox, a problem that was only solved recently using the language of generalized symmetries. Here we demonstrate a quantum spin chain analogue of magnetic monopole scattering on Quantinuum System Model H2. We implement a novel protocol for preparing a localized quasiparticle wavepacket on top of the ground state. By combining this protocol with time evolution across a duality defect, we efficiently convert local particles into non-local string-like excitations. We demonstrate this particle-to-string conversion in the transverse-field Ising model and a symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase of the cluster model. Our results establish duality defects and generalized symmetries as practical resources for preparing and probing non-local excitations on quantum hardware.

Oliver O'Brien, ..., Henrik Dreyer, Frank Verstraete

item.title: [7★] Demystifying Graviton Detection
item.author: Igor Pikovski
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 7 ★

Authors: Igor Pikovski

arXiv ID: 2611.07447 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Detecting single gravitons is possible through the extraction of discrete energy quanta from passing gravitational waves. For decades, this was considered hopeless, with estimates suggesting a detector the size of Jupiter. Here, I explain how these earlier estimates relied on the highly inefficient electron ionization process, while the absorption through the full mass quadrupole of a macroscopic system can bring graviton detection within experimental reach. Operating in the LIGO frequency band solves the challenges of graviton sources and noise suppression, allowing gravitons to be extracted from known passing gravitational waves and detection events to be heralded by classical gravitational-wave observations. Combined with the ability to resolve single energy quanta in macroscopic systems, such as in quantum acoustics, this opens a realistic path toward graviton detection. I also discuss the general limitations of particle detection in establishing an underlying quantum theory, illustrated by an energy-nonconserving semiclassical alternative. Nevertheless, the semiclassical alternative is not standard classical wave physics, and extracting E=ℏωE=\hbar\omega from a passing wave constitutes bona fide particle detection. This opens the way not only to the first detection of individual gravitons, but also to experimentally probing linearized quantum gravity and the graviton counting statistics of gravitational waves.

Igor Pikovski

item.title: [7★] Structured Quantum Hardness from Unstructured Assumptions
item.author: Xiao Liang, Takashi Yamakawa, Chak Fai Yung
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 7 ★

Authors: Xiao Liang, Takashi Yamakawa, Chak Fai Yung

arXiv ID: 2611.07413 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Whether useful structured hardness can arise from unstructured assumptions is a fundamental question in complexity and cryptography. The longstanding Bennett-Gill question asks whether NP∩coNP\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP} remains hard relative to a random oracle; [GIKKLS, STOC 2023] recently gave a conditional affirmative answer in the classical setting. We establish the quantum analogue: if UP⊈BQP\mathsf{UP}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}, then NPO∩coNPO⊈BQPO\mathsf{NP}^{O}\cap\mathsf{coNP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}^{O} with probability 11 over a random oracle OO. Beyond extending the classical result, this separation has a distinctly quantum significance: Shor's algorithms defeat canonical number-theoretic hardness candidates, while lattice assumptions and other leading post-quantum cryptographic assumptions do not directly supply hard languages with two-sided classical certification on every input. Our conditional oracle separation provides evidence that such structured quantum hardness can nevertheless arise from unstructured sources. Complementing this result, we rule out fully black-box quantum reductions of worst-case quantum hardness in NP∩coNP\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP} to post-quantum injective one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation. This barrier excludes a broad class of black-box approaches to deriving structured quantum hardness from generic cryptographic primitives, providing partial evidence that the non-black-box techniques in our first result are essential.

Xiao Liang, Takashi Yamakawa, Chak Fai Yung

item.title: [7★] Dithered Belief Propagation for Real-Time Quantum Memory Decoding
item.author: Zhengyu Cai, ..., Bokun Zhao, Warren J. Gross
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 7 ★

Authors: Zhengyu Cai, ..., Bokun Zhao, Warren J. Gross

arXiv ID: 2611.07144 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We introduce dithered belief-propagation decoding for circuit-level quantum memory to mitigate the oscillations and trapping behavior that limit standard belief-propagation (BP) decoders for qLDPC codes. Our approach combines a quantum-adapted sign-flip mechanism with chained randomized prior perturbation. Evaluated under circuit-level noise on the distance-11 rotated surface code and the distance-12 bivariate-bicycle code, the proposed dithered decoder significantly outperforms BP and BP+OSD+CS-10. The proposed decoder achieves accuracy comparable to or better than state-of-the-art Relay-BP, especially at higher physical error rates, while trading a moderate increase in additions for about 98% fewer multiplications on average and eliminating node-level RNGs. These results suggest that dithering is a promising approach toward real-time decoding of quantum memories.

Zhengyu Cai, ..., Bokun Zhao, Warren J. Gross

item.title: [5★] Quantum enhanced beam displacement estimation: sensitivity limits, optimal probes, and measurement schemes
item.author: Balázs Novák, ..., Emre Köse, Manuel Gessner
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 5 ★

Authors: Balázs Novák, ..., Emre Köse, Manuel Gessner

arXiv ID: 2611.08427 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We investigate the ultimate sensitivity limits for measuring small transverse beam displacements and identify optimal strategies that attain them, using the framework of mode parameter estimation. We contrast two families of states with different resource constraints, using Hermite-Gauss and Laguerre-Gauss mode pairs. First, for fixed total photon number states, the optimal state is identified and we show that it asymptotically approaches a rotated NOON state. The sensitivity bound is compared to that of an asymptotically optimal pure Gaussian state with fixed average photon number. Finally, we propose concrete measurement schemes using the method of moments and show that the twin-Fock state may provide a viable alternative to the rotated NOON state for this task. Our work provides a broader benchmark for developing practical strategies for spatial sensing at the quantum limit.

Balázs Novák, ..., Emre Köse, Manuel Gessner

item.title: [4★] Disorder-blind Mpemba acceleration of quantum state preparation
item.author: M Nishanth, ..., Roopayan Ghosh, Jinzhao Sun
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 4 ★

Authors: M Nishanth, ..., Roopayan Ghosh, Jinzhao Sun

arXiv ID: 2611.08424 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Using the strong Mpemba effect to accelerate relaxation by initial-state design requires suppressing the slowest mode, which typically needs prior knowledge of the system. However, in disordered systems, this mode is sample-dependent, so a fixed preparation generally retains a slow-mode overlap. We show that a ``blind'' preparation, designed from the clean chain without knowledge of the disorder realisation or its distribution, can start farther from stationarity yet overtake a reference in typical samples of a dephased disordered XX chain. It requires only the chain geometry and the particle number. At strong dephasing, the density dynamics maps to a resistor chain, and an exact inverse-generator identity links the residual overlap to the spatial resistance profile. We find two distinct thresholds: a finite mean resistance suffices for diffusion, but the residual overlap decays as L−1/2L^{-1/2} with chain length LL only when the resistance variance is finite; rare weak links slow this decay. We predict the fraction of samples in which the blind preparation wins, which is an ensemble-level measure of its reliability. Finite-size calculations support both scaling regimes with interactions at strong dephasing. We give preparation circuits and a density readout for the residual overlap.

M Nishanth, ..., Roopayan Ghosh, Jinzhao Sun

item.title: [4★] Accelerating Quantum-Classical Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo with Shadow-Trained Neural Quantum States
item.author: Justin Provazza, ..., Martin Roetteler, Luning Zhao
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 4 ★

Authors: Justin Provazza, ..., Martin Roetteler, Luning Zhao

arXiv ID: 2611.08129 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum-classical auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (QC-AFQMC) uses a trial state prepared on a quantum computer to improve the accuracy of the classical AFQMC algorithm. State-of-the-art QC-AFQMC represents this state with matchgate shadows, so every trial-walker overlap and local energy must be averaged over many snapshots, making this classical computation a bottleneck. Here we distill the matchgate shadow data into a symmetry-constrained, noise-aware, autoregressive transformer neural quantum state (NQS). Used as the AFQMC trial state, the NQS evaluates overlaps, force biases, and local energies without repeatedly summing over the matchgate shadows. For a nickel-catalyzed oxidative-addition reaction, the noise-awareness of our NQS design successfully recovers the ideal-upCCD AFQMC barrier and reaction energy within statistical uncertainty, while standard QC-AFQMC execution with the same shadow data yields qualitatively inaccurate results as a result of hardware noise. Since the shadow data are needed only for training, the estimated classical cost for the nickel system falls by approximately 99% relative to our previous QC-AFQMC implementation.

Justin Provazza, ..., Martin Roetteler, Luning Zhao

item.title: [4★] Efficient Pauli Truncation from Operator Stabilizer Rényi Entropy
item.author: Haihui Wang, Yongming Li
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 4 ★

Authors: Haihui Wang, Yongming Li

arXiv ID: 2611.07545 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Operator stabilizer Rényi entropy (OSE) quantifies the magic of Heisenberg operators and serves as a diagnostic of their compressibility in the Pauli basis. We establish rigorous bounds showing when an operator can be efficiently approximated by Pauli truncation in terms of the scaling of its OSE. Specifically, we prove that volume-law scaling of OSE for α≥1\alpha\geq1 prevents efficient Pauli truncation from reproducing expectation values for all states at sufficiently small fixed error. On the other hand, logarithmic growth of OSE for 0<α<1/20<\alpha<1/2 guarantees efficient Pauli truncation approximability uniformly over all states. A counterexample shows that this sufficient range cannot be extended on the basis of OSE scaling alone. If we restrict to correlations over suitable low-average state ensembles, then the sufficient range extends to 0<α<10<\alpha<1. We further derive cumulative error bounds for iterative Pauli propagation and approximation guarantees for fixed-order out-of-time-ordered correlators. Moreover, under an independent-sign assumption, we show that logarithmic OSE for 0<α<10<\alpha<1 guarantees efficient Pauli truncation with the prescribed accuracy for all input states with high probability. Our results provide a theoretical framework for understanding when operator magic constrains or enables efficient Pauli truncation and for guiding the development of classical simulation methods.

Haihui Wang, Yongming Li

item.title: [4★] Asymptotic advantage of quantum one-way and SMP communication for total functions
item.author: Dmytro Gavinsky
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 4 ★

Authors: Dmytro Gavinsky

arXiv ID: 2611.07318 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We exhibit a total Boolean function on n input bits whose bounded-error quantum simultaneous-message (and hence one-way) communication complexity is in O(\sqrt n), whereas its randomised one-way (and hence simultaneous-message) communication complexity is in \Omega(n). The same function admits a classical simultaneous-message protocol of cost O(\sqrt n) when the players share O(\sqrt n) EPR pairs.

Dmytro Gavinsky

item.title: [4★] Quantum simulation of classical RCL circuits via complexification and Schrödingerization
item.author: Huner Fanchiotti, ..., Rafael Gómez-Lurbe, Vicente Vento
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 4 ★

Authors: Huner Fanchiotti, ..., Rafael Gómez-Lurbe, Vicente Vento

arXiv ID: 2611.07300 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The decomplexification procedure establishes a mathematical equivalence between finite dimensional quantum dynamics and classical dynamics by mapping the complex quantum domain onto the real classical one. Its inverse process, complexification --- which lifts a classical dynamics to an equivalent quantum formulation --- is of great interest, particularly because it enables the quantum simulation of equations that are of classical relevance. In this way, one can prepare the solution of classical differential equations to be implemented using quantum computation tools. In the present work, we recall the decomplexification procedure and also discuss several distinct strategies for performing the complexification of classical equations, so as to obtain the corresponding quantum-equivalent dynamics.

Huner Fanchiotti, ..., Rafael Gómez-Lurbe, Vicente Vento

item.title: [4★] All Bell inequalities with a quantum advantage in the minimal scenario are self-testing
item.author: Mu-En Liu, ..., Victor Barizien, Jean-Daniel Bancal
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 4 ★

Authors: Mu-En Liu, ..., Victor Barizien, Jean-Daniel Bancal

arXiv ID: 2611.06997 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

In the minimal Bell scenario, all extremal quantum correlations are known, but the Tsirelson inequalities that delimit the quantum set remain poorly understood. We study which correlations can maximize a given Tsirelson inequality, and conversely, which inequalities are maximized by a given correlation. We show that every Tsirelson inequality with quantum advantage is maximized by a single, extremal correlation, and thus self-tests the corresponding realization. This characterizes all self-tests based on linear Bell inequalities in this scenario. We also show that at most a two-dimensional family of inequalities can be maximized by a nonlocal extremal correlation. We identify these as polygons for a family of correlations realized by qubit states of arbitrary entanglement. This allows us to deduce that the quantum set is not self-dual.

item.title: [2★] Quantum trajectory of a spin oscillator, continuous retrodiction beyond the Heisenberg uncertainty relation
item.author: Peiying Li, ..., Klaus Mølmer, Yanhong Xiao
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Peiying Li, ..., Klaus Mølmer, Yanhong Xiao

arXiv ID: 2611.08104 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The Heisenberg uncertainty relation in quantum mechanics limits the precision of predicting the outcome of measurements of any non-commuting observables. However, this restriction does not apply to retrodictive guessing of the outcomes of past measurements. Here, we experimentally demonstrate this using a spin oscillator consisting of 5.17×1010 5.17 \times 10^{10} rubidium atoms. Through weak continuous measurements, we monitor canonical spin observables ˆxA\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}} and ˆpA\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}} with [ˆxA,ˆpA]=iℏ[\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}},\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}}] = i\hbar. By combining information obtained before and after time tt, we retrodict the outcomes of measurements of ˆxA\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}} and ˆpA\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}} at time tt with variances that remain, concurrently over 1.4 hours, ∼\sim 1.01 dB below the bound set by the Heisenberg uncertainty relation. We also infer and demonstrate the ability to retrodict, with the same precision, the measurement outcomes for arbitrary quadratures of the spin oscillator. This brings interesting prospects for further research on quantum measurements, and for quantum-enhanced sensing that combines trajectory and entanglement strategies.

item.title: [2★] Approaching quantum limits in sub-Rayleigh resolution using phase modulation optimization

item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Chao-Ning Hu, Jun Xin, Xiao-Ming Lu

arXiv ID: 2611.08034 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Spatial-mode demultiplexing (SPADE) has made significant progress in incoherent optical imaging and has been implemented through various experimental approaches. Holography-based SPADE is widely used in proof-of-principle experiments because of its low cost, stable optical arrangement, and ease of implementation. However, its low photon utilization severely limits its practical applications. Alternating Fourier transforms and phase modulations can implement unitary optical transformations. Building on this idea, we use backpropagation to optimize the phase profiles of spatial light modulators (SLMs) and thereby design quantum measurements that are efficient in both information and energy. We study centroid--separation estimation for two incoherent point sources, using Fisher information or the estimation errors of an auxiliary neural network estimator as optimization objectives. As the number of SLMs increases, the optimized measurements approach the quantum limits characterized by the quantum Cramér-Rao bound and the information-regret tradeoff relation. With a few SLMs, our method can outperform direct imaging, showing its potential for superresolution imaging.

Chao-Ning Hu, Jun Xin, Xiao-Ming Lu

item.title: [2★] Optimal quantum metrology with restricted controls
item.author: Li Sun, Haoze Wang, Chong Chen
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Li Sun, Haoze Wang, Chong Chen

arXiv ID: 2611.07583 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum control can enhance sensing precision, but practical protocols are constrained by probe preparation and the available control resources. Optimizing the sensing protocol within these constraints helps establish what precision is experimentally attainable. We study quantum metrology from a fixed initial probe state under restricted Hamiltonian controls with bounded amplitudes. Building on Pontryagin's maximum principle, we formulate quantum Fisher information maximization at a prescribed interrogation time for multiple control channels subject to a weighted amplitude constraint. The formulation also accommodates stochastic Hamiltonian evolution and time-local master equations. A geometric description of sensitivity accumulation reveals the mechanisms underlying the optimized protocols. Two spin-1/21/2 examples demonstrate the resulting enhancement: time-dependent control outperforms optimized constant control in transverse-field sensing, while optimized waveforms improve upon CPMG pulses for AC-field sensing under strong colored noise. These findings highlight the importance of optimizing sensing protocols within available control resources to improve experimentally attainable precision.

Authors: Takuya Kubo, Hiroshi Nagaoka

arXiv ID: 2611.07462 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

For classical-quantum multiple access channels (cq-MACs) with two senders, we give several general expressions for the capacity region, valid for arbitrary sequences of channels. In the case of asymptotically vanishing error (ε=0\varepsilon=0), the capacity region is expressed in terms of spectral inf-mutual information rates. For every 0≤ε<10\le\varepsilon<1, the ε\varepsilon-capacity region is expressed in terms of a quantity defined through a linear combination of three alternative hypotheses. In particular, the outer bound of Kubo and Nagaoka (2015) is tight. Our results include the quantum counterpart of the general formula of Han (1998) for the classical MAC. The most important ingredient is the one-shot inner bound of Sen (2021), which we apply to each member of an arbitrary channel sequence.

Abstract:

The construction extends to other symmetries, including SU(N)SU(N).

item.author: Long Huang
item.content:encoded:

Authors: Long Huang

arXiv ID: 2611.08310 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Process tomography built on stabilizer codes compares the logical channel of a repetition code with a reference channel, and the decoder that produces that channel is almost always fixed to the standard minimum-weight one. We ask how many physical single-qubit Pauli gates the decoder actually needs when the measurement basis is fixed---the constraint under which the count is a resource rather than a bookkeeping artefact. Exhaustive enumeration of every recovery design for n=3n=3, 55 and 77 qubits, with rank decided by exact modular arithmetic at two primes, gives minimal counts of 00, 11 and 55 gates, against 66, 1010 and 1414 for first-order decoding and 66, 5050 and 308308 for full minimum-weight decoding. The count depends only on how many sites are corrected and never on which, so the two halves of the design problem separate. Correcting more sites is not monotonically better: at n=7n=7 full decoding loses three dimensions of rank, and under a calibration-residual floor the precision curve at n=3n=3 is U-shaped. The three-gate design is 9.59.5 times more precise than the standard six-gate decoder at the median of 4040 sampled working points, and more precise at every one of them (1.81.8 to 8888 times); the size of that factor belongs to the working point, the ordering does not. Reaching a 1010\u2009mrad rms error then costs 1.2×1071.2\times10^{7} shots in 6565\u2009s on a current superconducting device at a well-conditioned point, while n≥5n\ge5 stays out of reach for conditioning reasons rather than gate-count reasons. Finally, the optimal designs are not covariant under chain reversal: they separate the mirror pair of arXiv:2610.19779 by 1.3×10−31.3\times10^{-3} while leaving the Jacobian at full rank.

Authors: Fernando Almaguer-Angeles, ..., Marcin Pawłowski, Akshata Shenoy H

arXiv ID: 2611.07983 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum processors remain susceptible to crosstalk-induced effects despite the continuous evolution of their underlying hardware architectures. In this work, we experimentally investigate the effectiveness of crosstalk-induced attacks across six IBM superconducting quantum processors and one IQM processor. Our results demonstrate that such attacks can be launched across all the platforms, due to persistance of crosstalk, although their effectiveness varies significantly between devices. The probability of a measurement outcome flip in the victim qubits reaches a maximum value of 60%60\%. Also, it is seen that processors sharing identical coupling graphs exhibit different vulnerability profiles, indicating that connectivity alone is insufficient to predict attack efficiency. item.title: [1★] Probing Non-Abelian Topology through Quench Dynamics
item.author: Zhenming Zhang, Tianyu Li, Wei Yi
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Zhenming Zhang, Tianyu Li, Wei Yi

arXiv ID: 2611.07456 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quench dynamics offer valuable insights to topological matter, wherein the emergent topological phenomena serve as a dynamic probe to the topology of static Hamiltonians. While such a practice has been widely applied to detect the Abelian band topology or the Euler-class topology of band nodes, little is known regarding the quench dynamics of non-Abelian topological insulators in multiband systems, where the intertwining geometry of all eigenstates necessitates the description of noncommutative topological charges. Here we propose a quench protocol for non-Abelian topological insulators, so that the underlying topology can be systematically probed using dynamic signatures. Specifically, we develop a band-projection scheme to extract the gap-resolved topology from dynamic skyrmions in the emergent quasimomentum--time manifolds of the quench processes. These skyrmions are characterized by a series of gap-resolved dynamic Chern numbers, which enable us to reconstruct the full non-Abelian topology of the post-quench Hamiltonian, including the global non-Abelian topological charge and edge-state patterns under the open-boundary condition. Our proposal offers dynamical access to non-Abelian topology in multiband systems, and can be readily implemented using photons or cold atoms.

Zhenming Zhang, Tianyu Li, Wei Yi

item.title: [1★] Fidelity Determines the Minimum Error of Quantum Recovery
item.author: Dario Picozzi
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Dario Picozzi

arXiv ID: 2611.07344 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Even a recovery that maximizes worst-input entanglement fidelity can retain avoidable errors in subsequent measurements. Entanglement fidelity is the probability of passing a test of whether the state and its entanglement were preserved; infidelity is the probability of failing it. Operational error is the largest possible change in any measurement probability, quantified by the normalized diamond distance. For every finite-dimensional noise channel and fixed encoding, we prove that operational error and worst-input entanglement infidelity have the same minimum over all recovery operations. The proof constructs one final unitary (a reversible quantum operation) that makes any recovery's operational error no greater than its original worst-input entanglement infidelity. With a retained noise record, we determine the optimal error and characterize all optimal decoders subject to a Kraus-rank limit for each outcome. For a fixed decoded channel, a semidefinite program finds the optimal final unitary in the low-error regime. We characterize all optimal final corrections and show that, at a fixed error floor 0<ϵ<10<\epsilon<1, the operational optimizers' sensitivity to residual unitary errors of size ss is at worst of order s4/3s^{4/3}, while the canonical polar correction has quadratic sensitivity.

Dario Picozzi

item.title: [1★] Thermally-driven quantum reservoir computing
item.author: Thiago Werlang, Daniel Valente
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Thiago Werlang, Daniel Valente

arXiv ID: 2611.07187 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Heat generation limits computation, classical and quantum, from single logic gates to entire data centers. However, an in principle limiting physical factor can sometimes be turned into a resource. In reservoir computing, energy dissipation is what gives a reservoir its fading memory. Here, we introduce a paradigm where the data injection itself is encoded on the time-dependent temperature of a thermal bath. We derive an exact expression for the nonlinear response of any fixed readout, and prove a rigorous memory-nonlinearity trade-off which turns out to be a structural necessity, rather than a tunable dynamical regime, since the same coupling that injects data also enforces equilibration. We illustrate both results with a driven qubit, using a single free parameter, and with a pair of coupled qubits, where the breaking of a discrete symmetry opens a fifteen-dimensional space to a single observable, yet that observable alone recovers just over half of it. This refutes the misconception that large Hilbert spaces guarantee computational power. Our results relocate the memory-nonlinearity trade-off from the reservoir's dynamics to its measurement channel, pointing to observable choice and bath engineering (instead of Hamiltonian control) as the physical levers for a thermally-native quantum reservoir computer.

Thiago Werlang, Daniel Valente

Abstract:

We present an iterative scheme for generating finite superpositions of Fock states whose photon numbers differ by 2l2^l (2l2^l-step states). We derive an upper bound on the probability of generating such states. Based on the proposed class of states, we construct several bosonic encodings and compare their performance in correcting particle-loss errors. item.title: [1★] Quantum Noise Engineering in Advanced LIGO
item.author: Begüm Kabagöz
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Begüm Kabagöz

arXiv ID: 2611.07074 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Advanced LIGO is a gravitational-wave detector with extreme sensitivity, operating close to the quantum limits of optical measurement. The quantum noise in this system arises from vacuum fluctuations entering the interferometer readout port: phase-like fluctuations produce measurement imprecision, while amplitude-like fluctuations drive radiation-pressure back-action. In this review, we present an intuitive description in terms of complex fields and quadratures, and follow squeezed vacuum from its generation, through its interaction with the filter cavity and propagation through the interferometer, to the readout. We discuss how frequency-independent and frequency-dependent squeezing engineer quantum noise, and how correlations between optical quadratures map onto correlations between measurement imprecision and back-action. We conclude that LIGO is both a gravitational-wave observatory and a kilometre-scale platform for quantum measurement science.

Begüm Kabagöz

item.title: [0★] Quantum Knowledge Distillation: State-of-the-art, Applications and Open Problems
item.author: Aldana Al-Sulaiti, ..., Ahmed Farouk, Saif Al-Kuwari
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Aldana Al-Sulaiti, ..., Ahmed Farouk, Saif Al-Kuwari

arXiv ID: 2611.08461 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Knowledge distillation transfers predictions, representations, or other supervisory information between learning models and is increasingly investigated in quantum machine learning. Its applications extend beyond compression to cross-architecture transfer, circuit approximation, distributed learning, and classical deployment of models trained using quantum-derived supervision. This survey reviews these approaches using two complementary classification axes: teacher-student configuration and the role of quantum resources in the distillation process. Quantum-inspired methods are discussed separately from methods that simulate quantum computations classically or execute them on quantum hardware. We explain how measurement probabilities, expectation values, classical readouts, state overlaps, and circuit-level objectives support different transfer mechanisms. We then critically assess the presented results against baseline design, execution conditions, uncertainty, and resource costs. The evidence shows that distillation can improve selected quantum students, but benefits are task- and architecture-dependent, and several studies find negligible gains or even performance degradation. Evaluations on physical quantum hardware remain limited, with some testing individual quantum components rather than complete learning pipelines. Heterogeneous protocols and incomplete resource reporting prevent general conclusions about practical quantum advantage. We identify priorities for controlled benchmarking, noise-aware learning, reproducible evaluation, and efficient transfer between quantum and classical models.

item.author: Ke-Sean J.M. Peter, ..., Joshua D. Caldwell, Richarda Niemann
item.content:encoded:

Authors: Ke-Sean J.M. Peter, ..., Joshua D. Caldwell, Richarda Niemann

arXiv ID: 2611.08460 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum information systems such as quantum key distribution and quantum communications require bright, high-purity, stable sources of single photons to act as carriers of quantum information. As such, methods for obtaining single photon emitters (SPEs) in solid-state devices capable of articulating with quantum photonic circuits are a necessary obstacle that must be overcome. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes have been extensively studied as a host material for SPEs, though working in two dimensions is accompanied by engineering complexity. However, dimensionality can be reduced through the implementation of boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs). Here we investigate the potential of BNNTs as room-temperature SPEs using confocal photoluminescence microscopy and Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometry. Quantum emitters were found in BNNTs spanning the entirety of the visible spectrum, including spectral regions where SPEs within hBN have not been reported. Furthermore, each tube was found to possess multiple SPEs at varying emission wavelengths along the length, exhibiting lifetimes as fast as 0.5 ns, which is about two-fold faster than the fastest hBN SPEs. Additionally, we demonstrate that surface passivation/coating mitigates blinking events, therefore increasing the emitter stability. Thus, BNNTs can function as a single structure supporting a variety of multiwavelength SPE sources, while maintaining a compact radius of ~25 nm, making them ideally suited for deterministic placement and integration within nanophotonic devices such as waveguides and interferometric filters.

Abstract:

Compact gauge fields are powerful tools for controlling quantum dynamics and topological phases of matter. Non-compact gauge fields are particularly relevant for open systems, where particles or energy are exchanged with the environment. Here, we investigate the wavepacket and entanglement dynamics induced by an SU(1,1)\mathrm{SU}(1,1) gauge field. The wavepacket undergoes non-Abelian non-compact Bloch oscillations, in which the spectrum of an auxiliary one-dimensional quantum problem determines the transition between stable oscillations and unstable amplification. In the unstable adiabatic regime, the wavepacket probes an SU(1,1)\mathrm{SU}(1,1) topological defect, and its amplification is determined solely by a hyperbolic solid angle in Minkowski space. Threading an SU(1,1)\mathrm{SU}(1,1) gauge field through a bosonic tight-binding model yields the bosonic Kitaev model, whose volume or super-volume entanglement scaling is governed by the stability of the gauge field. We further propose an experimental realization of an SU(1,1)\mathrm{SU}(1,1) gauge field in a spinor condensate. Our results can be generalized to other non-compact groups and higher dimensions, providing a geometric framework for entanglement control, selective amplification, and engineering energy transfer.

Abstract:

Designing protein sequences that satisfy both secondary structure requirements and solubility targets remains challenging. We present DiffSequence-Q, a hybrid multinomial diffusion model conditioned on secondary structure at each residue and a continuous solubility target. To introduce quantum auxiliary supervision during training, we employ a quantum neural network (QNN) or quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold network (QKAN) as an auxiliary solubility prediction head over shared Transformer representations. Experimental characterization further demonstrated biological activity across three distinct protein families. Selected defensins exhibited pronounced inhibitory activity against Aspergillus niger, while xylanases and short-chain dehydrogenases exhibited substantial enzymatic activity. Together, these results support DiffSequence-Q as a framework for integrating structural requirements and solubility targets in protein generation, with experimentally demonstrated biological activity.

At χ∥/χ⊥=109\chi_\parallel/\chi_\perp=10^9, the computational basis gives an error of order unity for every shot budget, whereas a quantum Fourier transform on the poloidal register gives 1.3×10−51.3\times10^{-5}. The same barrier limits sample-based quantum diagonalization. The aligned measurement needs no time evolution, so the circuit is only state preparation and a five-qubit quantum Fourier transform. On a ten-qubit superconducting processor, the aligned basis gives a median error of 7.0×10−67.0\times10^{-6} with 768 shots, whereas the computational basis gives errors above 0.94 up to 1.2×1041.2\times10^4 shots. A trapped-ion processor shows the same behavior.

Abstract:

We construct a model for the response of a detector to vacuum fluctuations inside a massive hollow shell in a superposition of positions. The delocalized source mass gives rise to a superposition of spacetime geometries and their associated vacuum fluctuations. To describe this system, we employ the formalism of quantum reference frames to transition to a frame in which the source mass occupies a definite position while the detector is in a superposition of positions. This allows the dynamics of the detector to be analyzed using standard tools of quantum field theory on a definite curved spacetime. We compute the detector response for a wide range of configurations of the shell and detector positions and investigate how information about the quantum state of the shell is encoded in the response function, identifying features of the superposition that are effectively captured by the detector. In particular, we show that, under appropriate postselection, the response function exhibits interference patterns, and identify regions of the parameter space of the model in which the shell-induced contributions to the interference terms are maximized.

Abstract:

A detector inside a static spherical shell samples globally matched field modes even though its local geometry is flat. We construct the response of a compactly switched Unruh-DeWitt detector on a quantum-controlled pair of transparent spherical-shell spacetimes with common Arnowitt-Deser-Misner mass. A stipulated common-incoming scattering identification places the branch excitations in one Hilbert space. Their positive Gram matrix determines joint, conditional, and dephased detector responses at a finite common readout, retaining the physical detector-clock phase in the uncompensated protocol. An additional coherent phase-gate protocol compensates free detector-clock propagation while preserving the shell interaction response. For concentric shells the centered response is exactly ss wave. A common incoming direction basis extends the construction to a lab-fixed detector and displaced shell centers, preserving common-translation covariance. The equal-radius benchmark exhibits conditional changes of order 25%25\% without dark-port amplification. Combining radius and position produces an assignment-odd response that reverses under reflection and vanishes at the relational midpoint. The relative normalized-state contrast reaches 34.15%34.15\% among the computed samples; the relative clock-resolved probe-influence contrast reaches 8.09%8.09\% for the declared readout, while larger values belong to its separate shared-phase envelope. These effects already occur in the dominant-energy-condition-compatible core. They are relational, model-dependent detector responses, not a background-independent witness of quantum geometry. First-order coefficients have finite pointlike limits; finite-coupling statements are made only at a fixed shared regulator.

Abstract:

We study a chiral giant atom ultrastrongly coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide at two spatially separated points. At a relative coupling phase \pi/2, the total spectral density is independent of the distance between the coupling points, whereas its directional components are not. Authors: Alexandre Chaduteau, ..., Juraj Hasik, Titus Neupert

arXiv ID: 2611.07030 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases are the simplest example of quantum phases that cannot be detected by local order parameters. Their classification is by now well-established from multiple perspectives, a prominent one being via tensor network states. The practical question, however, is not mere classification, but detection: given the ground state of an interacting Hamiltonian and a symmetry group GG along with its representation, is there an efficient way to tell if the state is in a SPT phase with respect to GG? While there exist such practical tests in one spatial dimension (1D), methods in 2D have so far been restricted to finite-size systems or require an explicit form of virtual symmetries of the tensor networks representing the ground state. Here, we develop an agnostic and efficient method to detect interacting Z2\mathbb{Z}_2 2D SPT phases, using an infinite projected entangled-pair (PEPS) representation of the ground state. The method is agnostic to the symmetry representation in the virtual space of the PEPS tensor and applicable independent of the bond dimension of the tensors. Moreover, it is efficient as it does not require finite-size scalings: it works directly in the thermodynamic limit. We numerically demonstrate the procedure by mapping out phase boundaries away from fixed-point wavefunctions. We extract the SPT label cocycle data explicitly from the PEPS tensor.

Abstract:

The quantum Hamiltonian constraint vanishes for physical states. For separable Hamiltonians in minisuperspace, its vanishing variance yields a fundamental identity. Under the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, we derive the Matter-Geometry Fluctuation Relation, dynamically linking spacetime clock fluctuations to matter fluctuations. item.title: [0★] Nonlocal magic of fermions is bounded by entanglement fluctuations and is logarithmic for free fermions
item.author: Raghav G. Jha, ..., Alexander F. Kemper, Bojko N. Bakalov
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Raghav G. Jha, ..., Alexander F. Kemper, Bojko N. Bakalov

arXiv ID: 2611.07003 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Free-fermion states are classically simulable, yet, written as qubits, they typically carry extensive magic, the quantum resource that stabilizer circuits lack. Part of this magic is nonlocal: local unitaries acting separately on two parts of the system cannot remove it. If these local unitaries are restricted to Gaussian ones, the nonlocal magic grows linearly with the number mm of partially entangled fermion pairs. We show that this growth is an artifact of the Gaussian restriction: local Gaussian unitaries minimize the nonlocal stabilizer Rényi entropy for up to three pairs, but not from four pairs on. General local non-Gaussian unitaries that respect fermion parity take mm free-fermion pairs to fermionic Bell pairs with a fidelity that decays at most as 1/√m1/\sqrt m compared to exponential decay with Gaussian unitaries, so the nonlocal magic drops from linear to logarithmic in mm. The reason is statistical --- Bell pairs have equal Schmidt weights, that is, a fully degenerate entanglement spectrum, and a state can stay far from them only if its Schmidt weights are spread over many orders of magnitude. This spread is measured by the capacity of entanglement CEC_E, the variance of the entanglement Hamiltonian, and the nonlocal magic of any fermionic state grows at most logarithmically with CEC_E. Free-fermion pairs add to CEC_E independently, so CEC_E grows only linearly in mm, and this leads to the stabilizer fidelity decreasing at most as 1/√m1/\sqrt m. Almost all the magic of free fermions, including Hartree--Fock and BCS mean-field states, is therefore local.

Raghav G. Jha, ..., Alexander F. Kemper, Bojko N. Bakalov

item.author: Hanzhi Jiang
item.content:encoded:

Authors: Hanzhi Jiang

arXiv ID: 2611.07010 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Entanglement entropy (EE) is central to modern theoretical physics, yet its calculation in interacting theories with nontrivial time dependence remains challenging. In this thesis, we investigate the real-time dynamics of EE in strongly coupled quantum field theories (QFTs) using the Anti-de Sitter/Conformal Field Theory (AdS/CFT) correspondence. We first examine EE evolution in an exactly solvable two-dimensional conformal field theory (CFT) with an inhomogeneous sine-square deformation (SSD). We argue that the unconventional time evolution driven by the SSD Hamiltonian can be viewed as a change in spacetime foliation, producing new horizons in the dual three-dimensional bulk. Holographic EE calculations agree with CFT results in all comparable cases. We then study entanglement dynamics in generic chaotic quantum many-body systems. In the limit of late time and large regions, these dynamics are believed to admit an effective entanglement membrane description. In 2d CFTs, a degenerate membrane tension reproduces several entropy dynamics results, unlike the non-degenerate tension in higher dimensions. Using holography, we show that capturing reflected entropy in 2d CFT requires an additional degree of freedom in the membrane description. We further show that a conventional non-degenerate tension emerges when the CFT undergoes a relevant deformation, holographically dual to a planar Banados-Teitelboim-Zanelli (BTZ) black hole with scalar hair and an interior Kasner universe. We then develop a membrane effective theory for reflected entropy dynamics in higher dimensions. Finally, we apply the membrane theories for reflected entropy to study the time evolution of multipartite entanglement signals. We found that scrambling dynamics generate multipartite entanglement with rich structures.

Authors: Marek Rychetsky, ..., Anima Anandkumar, Natalia Ares

arXiv ID: 2611.06994 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Gate-defined semiconductor quantum dots are promising building blocks for scalable spin-based quantum processors, however their operational properties depend on several fabrication and control parameters, such as lithographic gate layout and applied voltages. Existing device architectures have been refined through repeated fabrication and experimental testing, producing layouts that support reliable device operation. However, this process does not exhaustively explore the design space, limiting the ability to obtain qubits with targeted properties. We address these challenges by presenting a differentiable inverse co-design framework for electrostatically defined quantum dots that jointly optimises gate voltages and the gate electrode layout. A semiclassical Thomas--Fermi electrostatic simulator provides reference data for a Fourier neural operator (FNO) surrogate, which predicts the two-dimensional charge-density field. The desired spatial distribution of the confined charge defines the target quantum-dot geometry for inverse design. The FNO reproduces charge densities with a relative L2L^2 test error of just 0.6\% and enables millisecond-scale differentiable evaluations. Relative to the CPU-based physics simulator, the FNO achieves a 17,000-fold speed-up on GPU for a single design, with further performance gains enabled by batched inference. When embedded in a gradient-based design loop with fabrication constraints, the FNO can produce both vertically and horizontally elongated double-dot confinement geometries from the same initial conditions. The ability to engineer these distinct confinement configurations demonstrates control over quantum-dot shape and position, providing a route towards designing devices with distinct qubit-relevant operating properties prior to fabrication.

Abstract:

Spin triangles are promising systems for defining and manipulating scalar degrees of freedom, such as chirality, partial spin sums, or combinations between the two. Here we extend this analysis to dimers formed by pairs of spin triangles, coupled by exchange or dipolar interactions. We show that the weak-coupling limit warrants the introduction of an effective two-qubit picture, and derive the expressions of the related Hamiltonians as a function of the underlying physical interaction between the triangles.
